title: Name the parts before the process
statement: Teach the names of a system's parts before explaining how they work together, so learners are not identifying parts while following their relations.
example: Teaching the part names first has a median effect size of about 0.75 to 0.92.
detail: The grade-7 science visual design guide pre-trains names before teaching a process, because a learner cannot follow relations among parts while also identifying those parts for the first time, and naming first reduces the processing the later explanation needs (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g7-science/brainlifts/video-visuals-human-v0.1.md`, lines 156-165). It cites pre-training effects with a median around d=0.75–0.92 (Mayer & Pilegard), and its example identifies the cell membrane, nucleus and mitochondrion before explaining how the membrane controls exchange. Its storyboard rules split naming from the process explanation whenever more than about three to five new labels would appear at once (line 259).
against: The guide expects pre-training, like signalling and segmenting, to add most when prior knowledge is low (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g7-science/brainlifts/video-visuals-human-v0.1.md`, lines 244-245), and its three-to-five-label limit is an operating heuristic.

evidence.quote: **Evidence.** Pre-training effects have a median around *d*=0.75–0.92 [18].
A learner cannot follow relations among parts while also trying to identify those parts for the first time.
Show about 3–5 concurrent new labels at most; otherwise split naming from process explanation.

citations.ref: Mayer & Pilegard, Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning
